title: The Big Parade

evidence.note: A full-text search of the Catalog of Copyright Entries, Third Series, Motion Pictures volumes for Jan-Dec 1952, Jan-Dec 1953 and Jan-Dec 1954 (archive.org — the complete 1909-Act 28th-year renewal window for a 1925 publication) found no genuine renewal for 'The Big Parade' in any of the three years; the only hits were an unrelated newsreel clip ('Greek independence celebrated in New York with big parade', 1952) and an unrelated musical about the California Gold Rush. If the film was genuinely never renewed, its real free date is a 28-year non-renewal lapse around 1954, not a 95-year term expiring in 2021 — but either way it has been public domain for decades.
evidence.source: Catalog of Copyright Entries, Third Series, Motion Pictures, Jan-Dec 1952 / 1953 / 1954 (archive.org)

evidence.note: Independently of the renewal question above: published 1925, the 95-year US copyright term ceiling for any 1925 work (renewed or not) expired at the end of 2020, so the film is public domain in the US by 1 January 2021 at the very latest regardless of how it got there.
evidence.source: Duke Center for the Study of the Public Domain, Public Domain Day 2021

evidence.note: The 1925 release had an original score credited to William Axt and David Mendoza; as a work published in 1925 it is also past its US term. Modern DVD and Blu-ray copies, however, carry a newer score (Carl Davis wrote one for the film in the 1980s). That recording and composition are separate protected works, not covered by the film's public-domain status.

Plain note, no outside citation located for this specific claim: the story was written by Laurence Stallings, a World War I veteran, for the film itself (scenario by Harry Behn, intertitles by Joseph W. Farnham). It is not an adaptation of an earlier published book or play, so there is no separate source work to clear. It was created for and published with the 1925 film, so it shares the film print's own public-domain status above regardless of the exact renewal mechanism.

Modern home-video releases of the film use a contemporary score in place of the original Axt/Mendoza score. A faithful restoration adds no new US copyright, but a new score or newly made titles on a given release can be protected. Check which version you are copying.

renewal_search.negative_result: No genuine renewal found in a full-text search of the 1952, 1953 and 1954 CCE motion-pictures volumes (see print layer evidence); the film is public domain either way (non-renewal lapse ~1954, or the 95-year ceiling expiring 2021 if it was renewed under a variant title we missed).

editorial:
The Big Parade is a 1925 silent war drama directed by King Vidor for Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer. John Gilbert and Renée Adorée star, and the story is by Laurence Stallings, a World War I veteran. It was chosen for the National Film Registry in 1992, and it heavily influenced later war films such as All Quiet on the Western Front (1930). The picture itself is public domain in the US. A direct search of the 1952-1954 Catalog of Copyright Entries motion-pictures volumes found no genuine renewal, so the more likely mechanism is a 28-year non-renewal lapse around 1954; even if a renewal exists under a variant title we missed, the 95-year ceiling for any 1925 work ran out by 1 January 2021 at the latest. Either way it has been free for decades.

The trap is the music, not the images. The original Axt/Mendoza score belongs to the 1925 release, but the DVD and Blu-ray editions use a later score. Carl Davis composed one for the film in the 1980s, and a modern score recording is a separate protected work. Lift the picture from a source whose soundtrack you have checked, or add your own music. The story layer has no outside source to worry about.
faq: Can I reuse footage from The Big Parade in my own video?

In the US, yes for the picture itself: the 1925 film's copyright term has expired. Take the footage from a copy whose music you have checked. Do not carry over a modern score from a DVD or Blu-ray, and do not rip copy-protected discs, which can breach 17 U.S.C. 1201.
Is the music in The Big Parade also free to use?

Not necessarily. The original 1925 score credited to William Axt and David Mendoza is itself an old work. A newer score added to a modern release, such as Carl Davis's, is a separate protected work. Use a score-free copy or clear the music separately.
